name: Clomiphene
lead: Clomiphene citrate (brand name Clomid, also Serophene) is an oral selective estrogen receptor modulator. It is approved in the US for ovulatory dysfunction in women who want to become pregnant, particularly those with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) [1][22]. In men it is prescribed off-label for low testosterone, as a way to raise the body's own output rather than replace it from outside [2].

In looksmaxxing and bodybuilding communities, clomiphene is discussed under the label 'tmaxxing' (raising testosterone) and as post-cycle therapy after anabolic steroids. The appearance chain proponents describe is that higher natural testosterone supports muscle mass, leanness, body hair, jaw and facial structure changes tied to androgens, and drive for training, while keeping the testes active and sperm production intact [2][3][22]. Users also compare it with enclomiphene, one of its two isomers, and one 2024 thread says enclomiphene raised testosterone more with fewer side effects [4][23].

A 2022 systematic review of clomiphene in men with hypogonadism covered 19 studies, four of them randomized, and assessed hormone levels, symptoms, metabolic profile and safety [2]. The label lists ovarian enlargement and vasomotor flushes as the most common adverse events and warns of visual symptoms that are usually reversible but may be irreversible [1]. The drug is prescription-only and is on the World Anti-Doping Agency prohibited list [22].
infobox: Synthesized 1956 by Frank Palopoli and colleagues at William S. Merrell Company [22]

paras: Women: the US label's indication is ovulatory dysfunction, and PCOS is named among the conditions most likely to respond.[1] Clomiphene was long the first-line drug for ovulation induction in PCOS. A 2014 randomised trial found letrozole superior to clomiphene for live birth in PCOS, and later meta-analyses and a Cochrane review compare the two.[6][7][8][9] Randomised trials have also tested clomiphene with acupuncture and in stair-step protocols.[10][11]

Men: a systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated clomiphene as off-label therapy for male hypogonadism, noting that exogenous testosterone suppresses the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis and spermatogenesis, which clomiphene is intended to avoid.[2]

Appearance-related use centres on raising testosterone for muscle, body composition and masculine traits, and on recovering natural testosterone after anabolic steroid cycles. On looksmax.org one poster states that clomid is taken after a cycle rather than cycled; another asks whether it could replace injecting testosterone, and a reply says it boosts testosterone but must be taken indefinitely and exogenous testosterone will always be better.[3]

Chemists at the William S. Merrell Chemical Company, led by Frank Palopoli, synthesized clomiphene in 1956, and a US patent followed in November 1959 [22]. It was studied in advanced breast cancer from 1964 to 1974 but was not pursued for extended use because of concerns about desmosterol accumulation [22]. The FDA approved it in 1967 under the brand name Clomid; it appears on the WHO Essential Medicines List, and its introduction is often credited with opening the modern era of assisted reproduction [22]. Ownership of the product passed through several companies including Dow Chemical, Hoechst, Aventis and Sanofi [22].

Through the 2000s and 2010s, trials moved the first-line position in PCOS toward letrozole, while clomiphene remained widely used [6][7][9]. For men, the idea of using clomiphene to raise testosterone while keeping fertility drew on the observation that blocking estrogen feedback raises LH and FSH [2]. The enclomiphene isomer was developed by Repros Therapeutics under the name Androxal; in January 2018 the European CHMP recommended refusing marketing authorisation for secondary hypogonadism, and development was discontinued in April 2021 [23].

The US label reports ovarian enlargement (13.6%), vasomotor flushes (10.4%), abdominal-pelvic discomfort and nausea among adverse events above 1% in studies of 8,029 patients, and warns of visual disturbances such as blurring or scintillating scotomata that increase with total dose or treatment duration; the label says cases of prolonged disturbance have been reported and they may be irreversible.[1] It is contraindicated in pregnancy; human data do not suggest a higher congenital anomaly risk, but animal studies showed embryo-fetal loss and malformations.[1]
In T Nation threads, men prescribed clomiphene for low testosterone or fertility report variable experiences, including increased libido in some and, in one thread, loss of libido.[13][14][15]

Wikipedia lists reversible ovarian enlargement (over 10 percent of women) as the most common effect, with headaches, hot flashes and visual disturbances less often, and rare reports of raised triglycerides, hepatitis, reversible hair loss and ovarian hyperstimulation [22]. Contraindications include pregnancy, liver disease and unexplained uterine bleeding [22]. Across 1,403 people in phase 2 and 3 enclomiphene studies, the most common events were headache (1.6 percent) and hot flush (1.1 percent), with rare thromboembolic events and one fatal stroke [23].

As a SERM, clomiphene blocks oestrogen receptors in the hypothalamus and pituitary, which raises gonadotropin release and, in men, stimulates testicular testosterone production.[2] Enclomiphene is one of its two isomers, studied separately in trials of men with secondary hypogonadism.[16][17][4]

Clomiphene is a mixture of two stereoisomers: enclomiphene, which is described as the pro-androgenic component with a half-life of about 10 hours, and zuclomiphene, the pro-estrogenic component that persists for days to weeks [22]. Enclomiphene has been developed separately as a single-isomer drug for male secondary hypogonadism [23].

Oral bioavailability is described as high (over 90 percent). The drug is metabolised mainly in the liver by CYP2D6 and undergoes enterohepatic recirculation, with an elimination half-life of about 4 to 7 days and onset of effect around 5 to 10 days into a course. Genetic variation in CYP2D6 contributes to different responses between individuals [22].

In women, the 2014 NEJM trial found letrozole produced more live births than clomiphene in PCOS [6]; a 2023 meta-analysis, a 2022 Cochrane review and a 2019 meta-analysis in unexplained infertility compare the two drugs [7][8][9]. A 2017 JAMA trial tested acupuncture and clomiphene in Chinese women with PCOS [10], and a 2023 trial compared stair-step protocols [11]. The 1998 and 2007 NEJM trials examined metformin with clomiphene [20][21].

In men, the 2022 systematic review of 19 studies (four randomized, 15 observational) assessed serum hormones, symptoms, lipid profile and safety in hypogonadal men receiving off-label clomiphene [2]. Enclomiphene was examined in registered phase 3 trials of men with secondary hypogonadism, including a 499-participant safety study and a 300-participant extension [16][17]. Wikipedia summarises enclomiphene studies from 2013 to 2019 reporting increased testosterone alongside raised LH and FSH, and sperm counts maintained [23].

No trials were identified of clomiphene for cosmetic aims in healthy men, for height in adolescents, or as post-cycle therapy after anabolic steroid use. Registered work also includes an anti-doping metabolism study [18].

Looksmax.org threads cover how clomid works and whether it must be cycled, comparisons with enclomiphene for use alongside MK-677 or Anavar post-cycle therapy, and requests from a self-described 15-year-old to buy it without a prescription after parents and a doctor declined.[3][4][5] T Nation users on testosterone therapy or fertility treatment describe starting clomiphene under physician guidance and compare outcomes.[13][14][15][19]

On looksmax.org, the best-known tmaxxing framing is that clomiphene is taken after a cycle and that natural testosterone is raised but 'exogenous T will always be better' [3]. A thread built on a 2024 article claims enclomiphene beats clomiphene and suggests it as an addition to other compounds [4]. Questions about acquiring clomiphene without a prescription, including from a self-described 15-year-old, recur and prescribers are described as declining [5]. T Nation threads from men on physician-supervised therapy discuss libido changes, restarting treatment, and combining it with other protocols [13][14][15][19].

Clomiphene is prescription-only in the US and elsewhere, and male use is off-label [1][2]. The World Anti-Doping Agency prohibits it in category S4, and it can appear in black-market products; athletes have also tested positive after eating contaminated poultry or eggs [22]. An anti-doping metabolism study of clomiphene has been registered [18]. Enclomiphene has no approved drug label; the FDA has discussed it in the context of pharmacy compounding, comparing it with testosterone replacement [23].

Related approaches discussed alongside clomiphene include injected testosterone replacement, hCG, the SERM tamoxifen (used for gynecomastia and post-cycle recovery), enclomiphene, and aromatase inhibitors. Women's fertility care compares clomiphene with letrozole and metformin [6][9][20][21].

lore.intro: Clomiphene is discussed as a testosterone-boosting alternative to injected testosterone and as post-cycle therapy, with enclomiphene debated as a cleaner option.[3][4]

claims.claim: Clomid raises natural testosterone without injections
claims.believers: Posters say it boosts endogenous testosterone and can serve 'tmaxxing' in place of injecting, while noting it has to be taken long term [3].
claims.experts: A systematic review of 19 studies in hypogonadal men assessed hormone levels and symptoms, describing the use as off-label [2].

claims.claim: Enclomiphene raises testosterone more than clomiphene with fewer side effects
claims.believers: A poster cites a September 2024 article comparing the two [4].
claims.experts: Enclomiphene was studied in registered phase 3 trials, but regulators in Europe declined authorisation for it in 2018 [16][17][23].

claims.claim: Clomiphene helps recovery after a steroid cycle
claims.believers: Users say it is taken after a cycle instead of being cycled [3].
claims.experts: Published male studies concern hypogonadal men rather than post-steroid recovery [2].

claims.claim: Clomiphene preserves fertility where testosterone does not
claims.believers: Posters and men on therapy describe it as the route that keeps the testes working [3][13].
claims.experts: The 2022 review notes exogenous testosterone suppresses the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis and spermatogenesis, which clomiphene is intended to avoid [2].

claims.claim: Exogenous testosterone will always be stronger than clomiphene
claims.believers: A looksmax.org reply states that outside testosterone is always better [3].
claims.experts: Clomiphene acts through the body's own feedback loop, so response depends on the pituitary and testes [2][22].

claims.claim: Teens can use clomiphene to start tmaxxing early
claims.believers: A self-described 15-year-old asks how to buy it without a prescription [5].
claims.experts: The drug is prescription-only, contraindicated in pregnancy, and the label warns of visual disturbances that may be irreversible [1]; no trials were identified in adolescent boys for cosmetic aims.

claims.claim: Clomiphene can reduce libido or mood in some men
claims.believers: A T Nation user reports libido loss after taking it [14].
claims.experts: The label lists adverse events including visual symptoms, and Wikipedia lists headaches and hot flashes [1][22].

card.summary: A fertility SERM that men use off-label to lift their own testosterone; some evidence in hypogonadal men, none for looks.
card.note: Label warns of possibly irreversible visual disturbances; male use is off-label.

quick.overview:
Clomiphene (Clomid) is a prescription drug for ovulation induction in women. Men use it off-label to raise their own testosterone, and looksmax.org discusses it for 'tmaxxing' and post-cycle recovery.

A 2022 review covers its use in hypogonadal men; no trials test it for cosmetic goals in healthy people.
quick.mechanism: It blocks oestrogen receptors in the brain's hypothalamus and pituitary, raising gonadotropins and prompting the testes to make more testosterone.
quick.risks: The label lists ovarian enlargement and flushes, plus visual disturbances that may be irreversible. Users report mood and libido changes. Prescription-only; teens asking for it without a prescription appear on forums.

chain: Oral SERM blocks estrogen feedback in the brain
Pituitary releases more LH and FSH
Testes make more testosterone, supporting muscle, leanness and androgenic features
angle.text: Men take clomiphene to raise their own testosterone, with the aim of more muscle, less fat and stronger androgen-driven traits, or to recover natural production after steroid use. Posters describe it as an alternative to injected testosterone that leaves the testes working.
